items.text:
Humans have been slurping and savoring noodles for centuries, with the first recorded noodle dish recorded during China’s Eastern Han period (25–220 CE). In fact, noodles would go on to become inextricable from ancient Chinese culture, with a wheat-based version emerging as a staple of the Han dynasty. Centuries later, noodle-making would hit Europe, transforming the cuisines of Italy during the Middle Ages and Germany in the early 18th century. The English word “noodle” itself goes back to the 18th century, borrowed by the English from the German “nudel.”


Whatever you call them, one thing remains certain: Love of noodles transcends culture and country. Jacques Cousteau once said that the sea was “the great unifier ... man’s only hope,” but did he ever consider the power of a steaming bowl of ramen? For this delicious guide, we’ve noodled on the best of the best around the world—places where mind-bending broths and eccentric histories collide to create unforgettable dining experiences.

1. Hrimnir Ramen 📍 Oslo, Norway


This Oslo eatery puts a uniquely Norwegian spin on traditional Japanese ramen, using seasonal local ingredients found from the fjords to the mountains. Opened by Norwegian-American microbiologist David Quist in 2019, Hrimnir places a special focus on fermented ingredients, with jars of preserved lemons, pickled plums, and pear vinegar lining the walls. The noodles are handmade in house with emmer wheat or tokornkveite, a heritage grain that gives them a uniquely nutty flavor.

2. Phở Hàng Trống 📍 Hanoi, Vietnam


Hanoi is considered the birthplace of Vietnam’s staple noodle soup, phở, and in the living room of home chef Ms. Minh, you’ll find some of the very best in the country. She’s been selling phở in Hanoi for decades but was forced to take her business inside in 2017, when the city started cracking down on street vendors.


At plastic tables, visitors to Ms. Minh’s home can enjoy traditional, northern-style phở (which has lighter, clearer broth than that in the south). She serves her noodles with jars of homemade chili sauce and pickled garlic, plus the option of dipping Chinese youtiao doughnuts in the hot broth.


3. Inari Soba Mansei 📍 Tokyo, Japan


This small soba shop dates back to the early 1600s, where it appears in the legend of Takuzousu, a Buddhist monk and kitsune, or shapeshifting fox-spirit. It’s said that Takuzousu frequented this very shop, where the coins he paid with supposedly turned into leaves once their magic had worn off.


You’d never know the restaurant’s legendary history from the outside, but inside, you’ll find a bronze bell from the original Takuzousu shrine displayed in glass. The menu, too, pays tribute to the kitsune by serving aburaage, a fried tofu believed to be foxes’ favorite food.

4. Pekin Noodle Parlor 📍 Butte, Montana


Pekin Noodle Parlor is the oldest continuously-operating Chinese restaurant in the U.S., opened in 1911 in what was once a thriving Chinatown. Passed down through the same family for generations, Pekin radiates old-school charm: A flickering, neon sign welcomes visitors into a dimly-lit space with orange booths and individual eating cubicles, where food arrives by trolley. The parlor’s main draw is the Chinese-American classic, chop suey, but it also serves up a mean chow mein and chicken noodle soup.


5. Mie Lethek Garuda 📍 Srandakan, Indonesia


In this traditional factory, cows turn a huge mortar that grinds dried cassava and sweet potatoes into flour for mie lethek, the region’s signature noodle variety. Mie lethek translates to “ugly noodles,” an apt name for these squiggly gray creations. But what they lack in beauty, they make up for in flavor: sweeter than your average noodle, with a pleasant, chewy texture.


Yasir Feri, Mie Lethek Garuda’s owner, is the grandson of the noodle’s creators, a Yemeni/Chinese couple who first opened up shop in the 1940s. After the cows have created the flour, Feri and his factory workers mix and press the dough by hand, then leave the finished noodles to dry in the sun before bringing them to the market. (The cows are also given sweet grass in return for their hard work.)

6. Pure Love Diner Bar 📍 Taipei, Taiwan


Colorful neon signs welcome you into this ’80s-themed den of vice (and noodles), complete with red lighting, disco balls, and antique furniture. The diner is an homage to Taipei’s old-school karaoke bars, known as “grandpa shops” for their older—and often flirtatious—patrons, though without any of the original bars’ suspicious activity.


Here, it’s all about enjoying the kitschy ambiance and chowing down on Taiwanese classics like braised pork over rice, oyster soup, fried chicken, and deep-fried noodles in satay sauce. Plus, there’s still a karaoke machine in the corner!

7. Fideus de Vermar 📍 Binissalem, Spain


This small town of Binissalem celebrates its rich wine heritage with the annual Festa des Vermar, which includes (among plenty of wine-based activities) huge cauldrons of short noodles, slow-cooked meats, red wine, and aromatic spices. This traditional local paella, called fideus de vermar, serves all 1,400 of the town’s residents during the festival, turning the main square into a lively picnic spot.

8. Bamonte’s 📍 Brooklyn, New York


Founded by immigrants in 1900, this family institution holds the distinction of being Brooklyn’s oldest Italian restaurant. It was once a favorite meeting spot of the New York mafia, as well as a setting for the fictional New Jersey mob in “The Sopranos.” Other (more law-abiding) Italian-Americans of note, such as Robert De Niro and Frank Sinatra, have dined here, and the restaurant honors its many famous guests with framed photos on the walls.


While New York City has grown exceedingly expensive, Bamonte’s has kept its Italian classics surprisingly affordable, and crowd-pleasers like the rigatoni alla vodka and linguine with red clam sauce keep people coming back year after year.

9. Khanom Jeen Pa Mai 📍 Phuket Town, Thailand


Thin white rice noodles called khanom jeen are a staple throughout Thailand, where they’re served with various spicy curries, meats, and vegetables. At this unassuming eatery in Phuket Town, customization reaches new heights with a lineup of everything from crispy dried fish to pickled mustard greens to pineapple slices.

10. Hawker Chan Soya Sauce Chicken Rice & Noodle 📍 Singapore


For about $3, you can enjoy a Michelin-star meal at this Singapore noodle shop. Owner and chef Chan Hon Meng first opened Hawker Chan as a food-court stall, where it became famous with his “secret,” Cantonese-style chicken marinade. The flavorful braised meat is served over char siew noodles, rice, or hor fun noodles with stir-fried veggies and braised eggs.


After Meng took home a Michelin star in 2016 (which he at first assumed was a practical joke), he turned Hawker Chan into a full-scale restaurant right next to where his humble stall once stood. Since then, other locations have opened in Thailand, Kazakhstan, Laos, and Malaysia, with more still on the way.

11. Lin Heung Tea House 📍 Hong Kong


Founded in the late 19th century, Lin Heung may just be Hong Kong’s oldest dim sum spot. It still does things the old-school way, too, with servers wheeling trolleys stacked high with bamboo steamers and calling out what dishes are up. Simply head over to the trolley and load up on what looks good to you, whether it’s rice noodle rolls, shrimp dumplings, pork ribs, or congee. The tea house can get quite crowded, so sharing a table with (or even befriending) fellow customers is simply a part of the experience.

12. Matsuka Seimen Noodle Factory 📍 Kurashiki, Japan


This gray shed functions mainly as a noodle factory, but during certain times of day, it changes gears to serve up freshly-cooked udon topped with eggs, scallions, and chili oil. Regulars swear by the kamatama: piping hot udon paired with nothing but a raw egg (cooked by the noodles) and a drizzle of soy sauce. Matsuka Seimen’s tiny kitchen also churns out a rich curry ramen made with fatty slivers of pork and soba noodles in a delicate green tea broth.


If you’re lucky, while you wait for your meal, you’ll witness the Matsuka family’s rather unusual noodle-kneading technique: A large tray of dough is covered in cloth and placed on the floor, where a family member walks all over it in special socks.

13. Bún Riêu Gánh 📍 Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam


On the busy streets of Ho Chi Minh City, Mrs. Mai Thi Lien serves up hefty ladles of simmering red broth from a massive pot on the sidewalk. Bún riêu, the noodle soup for which her restaurant is named, is made with rice vermicelli noodles and shrimp or pork mixed with crab paste, plus crispy tofu, huyet (coagulated pork blood), and herbs for garnishing. Mrs. Lien puts her own spin on the classic dish by pairing it with a tamarind fish sauce with sliced chili, giving it a distinctly southern Vietnamese flavor.

items.text:
Welcome to the Eater Cocktail Heatmap, focusing on the hottest new bar openings in New York every month.

Eater editors do thorough reporting on the most exciting restaurant openings to hit the city, as well as smaller openings worth having on the radar. In this monthly map, we narrow the field to cocktail bars that are drawing the most excitement, buzz, crowds, and early positive chatter, focusing on spots that have only been open for six months or less. When an Eater editor has already been to a place, we share insider tips on what to expect and what’s worth ordering as well.

New to the list in October: We’ve added Japanese cocktail bar Don’t Be Shy in Hudson Square; massive Chinese-leaning cocktail bar/restaurant/karaoke lounge Rewind in Long Island City; South Asian speakeasy Jam & Jaggery in the East Village; and retro bars FKA in the East Village and Velvet Cowboy on the Upper West Side. For now, we’ve removed Bar Chimera, Peek Inn, and Hidden Rivers Beer Garden.

For related drinking guides, check out Eater NY’s picks for the best cocktail bars, dive bars, and wine bars. And for more New York dining recommendations, check out the new hotspots in Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Queens. In need of an insider’s perspective on how to eat well, no matter where you are in NYC? Pick up our book: The Eater Guide to New York City.

The Jacob’s Pickles team turned its space on the Upper West Side (which relocated to Columbus Avenue) into Velvet Cowboy, a new 1970s Southwestern cocktail bar, in September. Find $5 bar snacks, like a take on the McRib sandwich, chili-cheese fries, and a huge funnel cake hanging from a stand.

A massive new restaurant-cocktail bar-karaoke lounge, Rewind, opened in Long Island City this September and is co-founded with AYS Hospitality, which runs Mr. Moto’s restaurant portfolio. The drinks menu, developed by beverage director Ken Chen, who had been at Taipei gastropub Indulge Experimental Bistro, took cues from tea, the Chinese zodiac, and the five elements. Tipsy Blossom represents fire signs and bitter elements, made with whisky, shochu, chrysanthemum, pear, hawthorn, licorice root, and goji berry. The food menu includes truffle-mushroom congee, Taiwanese fried chicken, and wagyu donburi. Per the name, people enter the space by pressing a “rewind” button on a retro boombox outside.

The team behind West Village cocktail lounge Dandelion expanded with Keepers, a new neighborhood-leaning bar and pizzeria, in July. Drinks, courtesy of Ricky Dolinsky (formerly of the View), include interesting Negronis such as the Black Forest, a drinkable homage to Ben & Jerry’s Cherry Garcia; spritzes; and frozens. Food-wise, find crispy tavern pies.

Bernie and Herb’s comes from a trio of 169 Bar alums who wanted to do a neighborhood spot that’s affordable and stays open until late. The bar opened in July, housed in the space that had been part of Coffee Shop, the Brazilian late-night icon in the area for 30 years. Look for drinks around $10 and inexpensive bar food like hot dogs, pulled pork sandwiches, and more.

FKA, which stands for “Formerly Known As,” is all about retro vibes since it opened in September in the East Village. Look for dollar East Coast oysters; dishes like lamb tartare, pimento cheese, Frito pies, and cheeseburgers; activities like pinball and Big Buck Hunter; and drinks like strawberry daiquiris, natural wines, and $8 beer-and-shot combos.

Chef Aarthi Sampath debuted a new speakeasy underneath her East Village restaurant Drāvida in September. Jam & Jaggery takes on the same South Asian foundation, with drinks like the Dirty Currytini with olive vermouth and curry leaves, and the Gola Chaat with shochu, yogurt, pomegranate, tamarind, herbs, and aloo bhujia, the latter of which is a spiced boiled potato snack. Sampath is offering some of her upstairs snacks, along with an Indian-ish burger.

The team, whose bar history includes Bar Valentina and Employees Only, took over the former Bandits space with a French-leaning bar. Bar Etienne opened in the West Village in August, with a very banana-y rum cocktail along with tomato martinis, chocolate Negronis, and wines. The bistro food menu includes steak au poivre and French onion-grilled cheeses, plus desserts created in collaboration with nearby Claude Bakery, such as tarte tatin and that chocolate cake.

New Hudson Square cocktail bar Don’t Be Shy is meant to evoke Tokyo’s stylish Ginza district since it opened in September. Head bartender Shinya Yamao, who worked at now-closed Piora and Tribeca sake bar Shigure, developed a Japanese cocktail menu with a special Trip to Japan menu available only at the nine-seat bar counter, exploring Japanese history and regionality, like the Edo, made with a potato-miso-flavored vodka and a sweet potato-Campari ice cube. Other drinks are available at the table seats, such as the Miyajima, which has momo nigori sake, red shiso, and lemon. Food includes wagyu and egg salad sandos and umami burrata with taro chips, pecans, dashi, and tomato sorbet.

Alas, Enid’s isn’t coming back, but the Greenpoint Fish & Lobster team turned its Greenpoint address into a new bar paying tribute to another shuttered neighborhood fixture. They opened Matches (a nod to Bar Matchless) in August, with $16 cocktails, along with burgers and steak frites.

Co-owners and couple Mercury Tin and Philip Dizard opened Tin’s on the Lower East Side as their ode to their life experiences. It’s a two-floor, New York-meets-Shanghai bar and restaurant that opened in July (and thankfully, the kitchen is fully open, serving those Shanghai-style dumplings). Drinks pay homage to those blending influences; see: an ode to the Dead Rabbit’s Irish coffee with a Shanghai dirty coffee twist.

A new cocktail bar devoted to all things rum opened in Williamsburg in April in the former original Gertie space. Echo Lake offers $12 daily daiquiris and a lager/rum shot combo cutely called Tiny and a Tot, plus seafood-centric plates like oysters with tepache mignonette and green coconut curry chowder. The new bar comes from beverage power couple Chloe Frechette (the former executive editor at Eater sibling site Punch) and Paul McGee, who cut his teeth at Chicago’s now-closed tropical bar Lost Lake. The duo is also featuring their own collection of liquid loot within the intimate basement rum bar, Undercurrent.

The team behind Mexican fine-dining restaurant Corima and burrito hot spot Vato opened a new bar in downtown Manhattan this April. Bar Chucho, a comparatively casual bar counterpart to Corima, offers fantastic drinks like the Desert Rain with sotol, along with lots of micheladas and familiar food like the carne asada-esque burger.

New Williamsburg bar Dokidoki, which opened in July, is just a fun meshing of Latin and Japanese cultures, courtesy of co-owners and cocktail vets A-K Hada, an alum of Please Don’t Tell and Existing Conditions; and Christian Suzuki-Orellana, a semifinalist on Netflix’s Drink Masters. With just a beer and wine license, they’re whipping up fun martinis and honeydew “margaritas” made with shochu, sakes, and local meads. The Japanese-Puerto Rican-Salvadoran bar snacks include a katsu sandwich made with cod on shokupan bread. It’s a small yet cozy space.

Brooklyn cocktail bar Grand Army alums Patty Dennison and Ally Marrone opened their own bar in Williamsburg in May, taking over what was the Ensenada space. The press release describes Kinda Nice as a mix of “late-night diner culture” and “dive bar spontaneity,” which translates to savory and sweet cocktails like the guava Negroni with malted milk and pisco; the Greek Salad martini with Tomato Crop vodka and a piparra brine; and a tequila drink with lime sherbet and a choice of blueberry or strawberry amaro and tequila. The duo also debuted their downstairs dive bar at the address, Shenanigans, with beers, highballs, boilermakers, and DJs (dancing is encouraged)

New Bushwick bar the Museum Bar + Gift Shop is meant to feel like a hella fun natural history museum, which opened in June. The space is covered in illuminated fossils, crystals, and dinosaur heads. The drinks list continues that thread, with the Insectarium, a Negroni-ish drink with insects; and the Ocean Life made with rum, coconut, limes, Curaçao, and cuttlefish ink. The on-site Gift Shop bar focuses on lower-ABV drinks with cafe touches, such as spritzes and milk punches.

Billy Durney was inspired by “one crazy night in Paris many years ago” to open this Brooklyn cocktail bar next door to his Red Hook Tavern, with “reinvented disco-era cocktails,” in May. That translates to vibrant Blue Hawaiians, Adam’s Appletinis, and creamy White Russians and Brandy Alexanders. And yes, there’s an iteration of that famous cheeseburger, too.

This new Gowanus spot, which opened in July, aims to fill the bar gap left by the address’s previous tenant, Dirty Precious, now with a 1980s look. Co-owners Robin Daily and Mike Brown met at Royal Palms Shuffleboard Club, where one worked and the other frequented, respectively. At Shania’s Max Bet, they’re serving up martinis, Midori sours, and beer-shot combos.

It’s a horse girl’s world: Co-founders and couple Elana Shvalbe and Michael Furac opened this new daytime cafe and evening bar in Red Hook in August, with a pony-loving aesthetic. Find gin martinis; a rye-and-rum Old Fashioned with peanut butter and bananas; and a High Life pony-shot combo for $10, along with an Eastern European-ish food menu including pelmeni and cured and smoked fish.

The Jacob’s Pickles team turned its space on the Upper West Side (which relocated to Columbus Avenue) into Velvet Cowboy, a new 1970s Southwestern cocktail bar, in September. Find $5 bar snacks, like a take on the McRib sandwich, chili-cheese fries, and a huge funnel cake hanging from a stand.

A massive new restaurant-cocktail bar-karaoke lounge, Rewind, opened in Long Island City this September and is co-founded with AYS Hospitality, which runs Mr. Moto’s restaurant portfolio. The drinks menu, developed by beverage director Ken Chen, who had been at Taipei gastropub Indulge Experimental Bistro, took cues from tea, the Chinese zodiac, and the five elements. Tipsy Blossom represents fire signs and bitter elements, made with whisky, shochu, chrysanthemum, pear, hawthorn, licorice root, and goji berry. The food menu includes truffle-mushroom congee, Taiwanese fried chicken, and wagyu donburi. Per the name, people enter the space by pressing a “rewind” button on a retro boombox outside.

items.title: London Is Calling at Soho’s Hot New Straker’s

This is Eater’s guide to all the new
items.text:
Thomas Straker’s namesake London hit makes its stateside debut in NYC this weekend. | Thomas Streat/Straker’s

This is Eater’s guide to all the new restaurants, bars, and cafes that have opened this week in October 2026 Throughout the month, we’ll update the list weekly (see: September, August, July, June, May, April, March, February, January). When we’ve been to a place, we will then include a few openings on our heatmaps (Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, cocktail bars) to let you know the ones we like. If there’s an opening in your neighborhood that we’ve missed, let us know at ny@eater.com.

October 7

Spotlight

Soho: London chef and internet butter evangelist Thomas Straker takes over the former Lucky Strike, Keith McNally’s now-closed Soho fixture, for his first restaurant outside the U.K. A late-September opening date for Straker’s was pushed back to Saturday, October 10. The New York restaurant centers on an open kitchen surrounded by steel and green stone, leather banquettes, dark wood, and warm lighting. Expect the modern British cooking style with Italian leanings that defines the Notting Hill original that opened in 2022. 59 Grand Street, at West Broadway

And the rest…

Brooklyn Heights: Brooklyn’s charming new Georgian restaurant Bebo, open since late September, pays homage to grandmas everywhere with comfort foods like khachapuri, vibrant dips, and crockets of soup in a cozy space surrounded by fringed lampshades, cottage curtains, and antique plateware. 145 Atlantic Avenue, between Henry and Clinton streets, Brooklyn

Bronx: After 14 years, neighborhood sports bar Triona’s closed its original location after the Chicago Bears game on Monday, September 28, but reopened next door on Friday, October 2, as Triona’s Vintage Sporting Club. The landmarked Scheffel Hall building dating back to the late-1800s was a German beer hall and restaurant and later housed the German-American Athletic Club and Fat Tuesday’s jazz club. Vintage sports memorabilia joins more than 20 screens and an updated Irish-leaning pub menu, with a continued love for the Bears and Michigan Wolverines. 190 Third Avenue, at East 17th Street

Chelsea: A chic taste of Verona landed in New York on Thursday, October 1, with the arrival of Italian wine bar and bistro Bar Lento. Lento, the Italian word for “slow,” features a brick-framed backdrop with a secret garden inside. The warm setup showcases a wine list of whites, bubbles, and pét-nats from Sardinia to Veneto to go along with seasonal plates like bruschetta and fluke ceviche in a citrus tomato vinaigrette. 158 Eighth Avenue, near West18th Street

Chinatown: Something Smells Fishy, a casual Japanese seafood counter that accepts walk-ins only, specializes in customizable kaisendon rice bowls topped with the likes of raw tuna, salmon, fluke, and uni. 95A Elizabeth Street, near Grand Street

Crown Heights: Brooklyn Surf & Soul, a new takeout spot serving seafood and soul food, opened on October 3. It’ll offer shrimp po’ boy sandwiches, whiting sandwiches, shrimp and grits, seafood boils, fried chicken, and more. 602 Nostrand Avenue, near Pacific Street

East Village: Table Mercato, Boston’s cult-favorite Italian sandwich shop that specializes in crispy chicken cutlets shoved between freshly baked focaccia, added its first NYC location in late September. Chef Jen Royle’s popular Sicilian and spicy vodka Parm sandwiches, priced in the mid-$20s a pop, commanded immediate long lines out front (open 11 a.m. until sell-out). There are also house-made chips, onion dip, and rainbow cookies. 214 E. 10th Street, between First and Second avenues

Financial District: Nationwide ramen bar Kyuramen debuted a trio of fast-casual spots on one 9-to-5 strip in NY on Thursday, October 1. Kyuramen Express slings ramen, udon, rice bowls, sushi, onigiri, and appetizers; Bao Dumpling is a Chinese takeout with a knack for dumplings; and Aokō Matcha offers specialty green drinks and desserts. Open daily from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. for dine-in, takeout, and delivery. 40 Gold Street, near Fulton Street

Lincoln Center: Prolific French chef Daniel Boulud returns across from NYC’s cultural hub in a big way on Thursday, October 8, with the opening of Brasserie Boulud — a consolidation of his closed Upper West Side restaurants (Bar Boulud, Boulud Sud, and Épicerie Boulud) into one massive, 10,000-square-foot flagship. The classically French-leaning Brasserie Boulud features the greatest hits from each dearly missed restaurant in one combined menu. Expect seafood towers, French onion soup, steak frites, lobster souffle, and boudin blanc, along with the return of Boulud’s cult-favorite DB Burger. 1900 Broadway, at Lincoln Plaza

Lower East Side: Australia’s popular and prolific Gelato Messina has made its American debut, with the opening of Softville on October 1. Continuing the city’s fancy soft serve moment, Softville will offer it, made using dairy from Ronnybrook Farm in the Hudson Valley, alongside an extensive and rotating menu of sauces and toppings. It also offers loaded sundaes, such as a birthday cake sundae featuring fior di latte soft serve, butter cake, strawberry pudding, “birthday crumble,” strawberry and white chocolate sauce, cream cheese chantilly cream, and sprinkles. A collaboration with Studio Jeremyville, the shop is described as an “art-led concept store,” in which Studio Jeremyville sculptures and other art will be on display. The art studio has worked with Messina since its early days, creating murals for its stores. 137 Orchard Street, between Rivington and Delancey streets

Lower East Side: Brazilian restaurant Iara opened on Friday, October 2, from chef Vitor Mendes, who previously worked at Brooklyn hot spot Theodora. Mendes cites a trip to his home country of Brazil following his father’s death as inspiration for the restaurant. Before it, he told Eater NY, “I thought that my own culture was rice, beans, and barbecue, as a lot of people might think.” At Iara, he’ll employ cassava in many ways: in the crispy cubes of tapioca served with yellowfin tuna and smoked biquinho peppers, in the vinaigrette paired with his hiramasi ceviche, in the fries that accompany his picanha, and more. 205 Allen Street, at East Houston Street

Park Slope: After shuttering his 120-year-old family bakery in Carroll Gardens earlier this spring, James Caputo is back in the baking business with Caputo Bagels, which opened Monday, October 5. The new bagel shop, a collaboration with Miriam owner Rafi Hasid next door, is all about hand-rolled sourdough bagels, open-face and breakfast sandwiches, as well a familiar take on the bake shop’s famed lard bread. 81 Fifth Avenue, near Prospect Place, Brooklyn

Red Hook: All-day diner and bar Vals debuted in Brooklyn at the beginning of October with a menu full of waffles, Denver omelets, blue-plate specials like spaghetti and meatballs, funnel cakes, and milkshakes. Located in the revived Fort Defiance, Vals’ name nods to the nearby Valentino Pier. Nicely priced drinks at the newly expanded bar include draft cocktails, well drinks, beer-shot combos, Negronis, martinis, and more. The new hangout comes from Victoria Viscusi, chef Allie Gassaway, and Laine Pelka, the latter two of which previously worked in the same space before. 347 Van Brunt Street, at Wolcott Street, Brooklyn

Theater District: Diner 24, the Gramercy greasy spoon known for its giant shakes, hot dogs, and burgers served by singing waiters, added a flagship corner location in the heart of Times Square on Wednesday, October 6. Located right under the historical Lambs clubhouse, the new 235-seat Diner 24 that’s open around the clock also hosts hourly performances from actors with Broadway backgrounds from a dedicated 20-foot stage upstairs. “Mamma Mia” and milkshakes, anyone? 1674 Broadway, at 52nd Street

Times Square: Southern food chain Kitchen + Kocktails by Kevin Kelley, which started in Dallas in 2020, opened its first location in New York City. The restaurant, which is the chain’s largest, will serve dishes such as Cajun crab cakes, fried seafood and chicken, smothered steak, jerk lamb chops, and shrimp and grits. The opening continues the restaurant’s national expansion. It also has locations in Atlanta, Charlotte, Chicago, Miami, Philadelphia, and Washington, D.C., and will soon be opening in Boston and New Orleans. 7 Times Square, at 7th Avenue and 41st Street

West Village: Camari Mick’s long-awaited Calabash, billed as an Afro-Caribbean bakery and brasserie, opened for daytime service on Friday, October 2. Running from Thursday to Sunday, daytime service will feature Mick’s acclaimed baked goods, including sticky buns, coconut canelés, and beef patty croissants, plus cornbread pancakes with salted maple sabayon. Dinner service begins on October 9 and will be available for a single 6:30 p.m. seating on Friday and Saturday nights via prepaid bookings. items.title: Fugu Film: Documentary “Gun Fish” Explores Secrets of a Risky Food Culture

items.text:
Many kinds of Japanese seafood are celebrated around the world, but fugu—the blowfish species famous for the deadly toxin they retain when not prepared correctly—may be among the most famous. A new documentary sheds light on the “gun fish,” named for its lethal power, and the culinary culture that has appeared around it.

A Perilous Delicacy

(© Gun Fish Film Partners)

The documentary Gun Fish opens at an official Tokyo facility dedicated to removing poison from fugu. At the time of filming in 2017, it was found in Tsukiji, before the world-famous wholesale seafood market moved to Toyosu. As you might assume from the name, this was a place where fugu, the general Japanese term for all varieties of blowfish, headed to market had their poisonous organs removed. In the off season lasting from spring through summer, it was also an exam venue for Tokyo’s fugu cook license.

Handling fugu is strictly controlled by rules set at the prefectural level. There is no national standard for acquiring or labeling the various licenses, but basically all are designed to ensure that cooks have the necessary knowledge and skills to serve fugu safely to the public.

The exam for obtaining a fugu cook license requires detailed knowledge of various fugu varieties. (© Gun Fish Film Partners)

Getting certified requires being able to identify different fugu species, differentiate the edible and inedible parts of each, and safely clean the fish. Fugu poison, a form of tetrodotoxin, is mostly concentrated in the liver and ovaries, but the poisonous parts can vary by species. Of the 70 species of fugu that live in the seas around Japan, 22 have edible flesh, while 18 have edible milt (testes), and only 11 have edible skin and fins. The road to becoming a pro fugu cook requires a vast amount of knowledge and experience.

While filming at the toxin-removal station, documentary director Uno Wataru’s great discovery was the chef-in-training Nameki Yukari, who became his film’s main focus. Just 23 years old at the time of filming, she first takes the screen near the very beginning of her studies, at which point she seems not to have absorbed any of her lessons.

Uno looks back on her progress. “As we were filming her training, my first thought was that we wouldn’t be able to use any of the footage. But two weeks later, it was like watching a totally different person handling the fugu. It was fascinating. I called up a friend who’d been helping with the filming and said, ‘We’ve got our main character. We’re on our way to a movie.’ I remember being really excited.”

Nameki Yukari identifying fugu species. (© Gun Fish Film Partners)

The Future of Fugu Fishing

The first half of the film shows scenes of Nameki’s intense training, interwoven with easy-to-understand explorations of fugu biology, culture, and history that sketch out this fish’s unusual position.

One bit of trivia mentioned is how Shimonoseki in Yamaguchi Prefecture became the national center for all things fugu. It stands near many fertile fishing grounds and fugu had long been a part of local cuisine, but the decisive moment came when it was the first place in Japan for the official ban on serving fugu to be lifted. That was the work of Japan’s first prime minister, Yamaguchi-born Itō Hirobumi (1841–1909), who greatly enjoyed a fugu meal in Shimonoseki. The restaurant where he ate it, named Shunpanrō, is also where the peace treaty ending the First Sino-Japanese War (1894–95) was signed. The lifting of that ban allowed for fugu restaurants to flourish in Shimonoseki and encouraged rapid development in fugu dressing and cooking skills.

Haedomari, Shimonoseki’s fugu-specialty market, opened in 1974. Fugu caught all over Japan are brought here and the poisonous parts removed before the fish are shipped out for further processing nationwide. Shimonoseki thus rose to prominence not as a fishing center for fugu, but a major logistics hub for the fugu industry.

The traditional “bag auction” at Haedomari Market. The buyers indicated their bids silently, using finger signals inside the bag. (© Gun Fish Film Partners)

Today, though, the once-uncontested strength of the “Shimonoseki brand” is on the wane. “Even as farmed fish now accounts for 90 percent of the market, the wild-caught fugu fishing grounds have been migrating further and further north, with many now caught in Tokyo Bay, Sotobō in Chiba, or the seas off Sōma in Fukushima,” explains Uno. “The shift away from shipping fugu all the way down to Shimonoseki has only accelerated in the nine years since we filmed. I think Shimonoseki itself is standing at a crossroads.”

Osaka’s Original Fugu

When speaking of fugu, Osaka stands alongside Shimonoseki as a must-mention. It is the largest consumer market in Japan, accounting for 60% of all the fugu eaten on its own. Many buyers bring it in directly from the fishing ports, making it cheaper for consumers. As a result, its reputation as a high-end fish is relatively unknown in the city. Osaka also has a lot of licensed fugu cooks, and over the years has adopted its own unique approach to licensing. Uno got officially registered as a fugu cook in Osaka in 2017, and saw for himself the difference from Tokyo.

Director Uno Wataru. (© Nippon.com)

“For example, in Tokyo, there is a fixed pass rate, and if you don’t hit the required line, they’re just like, ‘See you next year.’ But in Osaka, they train you until you have the knowledge you need. Rather than detailed prep skills, the focus is on being able to remove the poisonous parts. You’re expected to learn all the cooking skills that come after that in the kitchen. It’s a fitting philosophy for Osaka, which has so many fugu restaurants.”

Kushida Kōichi, the fugu expert behind Kushida Suisan at Tsukiji (now Toyosu) market. (© Gun Fish Film Partners)

At the same time, the Zenkoku Fugu Renmei (National Fugu Federation), which features prominently in the film, is promoting uniform licensing across Japan, since the lack of a single standard makes it difficult to get import restrictions lifted in the EU and other global markets. Their efforts resulted in the Ministry of Health, Labor, and Welfare releasing guidelines on eliminating variance in prefectural rules. Tokyo responded by easing the qualifications for taking the exam and the knowledge tested, while Osaka has moved from a training-based system to an exam-based one.

Shimonoseki’s annual Fuku (a local variation on the fugu name) Memorial Festival, which brings fugu professionals together from all over Japan. (© Gun Fish Film Partners)

The Meat of Fugu Cuisine

After viewers are given a crash-course in basic fugu knowledge in the first half, Gun Fish presents a heated debate around a core question in fugu food culture: What if fugu was made nonpoisonous?

The starting point is the taboo of eating the liver. The toxicity of fugu liver has long been common knowledge, but on hearing that it is also incredibly delicious, many people have apparently given in to temptation and lost their lives. One of them was famed kabuki actor Bandō Mitsugorō VIII (1906–75). The living national treasure’s 1975 death by fugu poisoning resulted in a law strictly punishing the sale of fugu organs.

A traditional Ishikawa Prefecture dish of pickled fugu ovaries, which are just as dangerous as the liver. The only way to make them edible is this traditional method of fermenting them for over three years in brine and rice bran. (© Gun Fish Film Partners)

But in 2004, a Nagasaki University research team investigating fugu poison succeeded in making farm-raised fugu poison-free, leading to an article in the English-language science magazine Nature. If fugu liver became safe to eat, it would surely mark a watershed moment in Japanese food culture.

Saga Prefecture sought to leverage this breakthrough in a local revitalization scheme. It applied to the MHLW for special certification as a Fugu Liver Zone, where people would be allowed to sell and eat nonpoisonous farmed fugu liver. Predictably, the National Fugu Federation and the city of Shimonoseki opposed the effort, saying a single accident could destroy trust in the nation’s fugu cuisine as a whole. The scheme has been rejected three times by the ministry and abandoned entirely.

The documentary takes up this liver-eating debate, introducing both the pro and anti sides as it explores the current state of fugu cuisine in Japan.

”I think if fugu weren’t poisonous, we wouldn’t have a movie. I see a certain Japanese-ness expressed in the opposing values that the debate brings to light. I wanted to show both sides equal respect, so I labeled them the ‘adventurers’ and the ‘custodians.’ Neither side is good nor bad; each is taking the stance of following through on their claims and their beliefs. And I find that really cool.”

Kamei Kazuhiro (right), owner chef of Kyoto restaurant Fugu Ryōri Tomoe, demonstrates the technique of slicing fugu sashimi. (© Gun Fish Film Partners)

Betting Their Lives on Fugu

The film introduces people working with fugu in all sorts of roles, each one sharing their own love of the fish. Their positions are all different, but they share the same ideals of broadening the dishes using this unique fish, preserving the culture of its cuisine, and nurturing it for the future.

Says the director: ”When I was editing the film, I grew convinced that bringing all of these people together into one film was something only I could do. That is one of the biggest things I learned through all this.”

Kitahama Kiichi, owner of Osaka’s Kitahachi restaurant and founder of the Fugu Museum, is one of the world’s leading fugu researchers. He insists that “Fugu brings people together.” (© Gun Fish Film Partners)

In all, a decade passed from the start of filming until the documentary’s completion, spanning the COVID-19 pandemic.

Uno laughs: “Before I started looking into it, I had the same image of fugu as most, that it’s this poisonous, high-class fish. I never imagined I’d get so into it! This must be the true danger of fugu!”

The Meat of Fugu Cuisine
After viewers are given a crash-course in basic fugu knowledge in the first half, Gun Fish presents a heated debate around a core question in fugu food culture: What if fugu was made nonpoisonous?

The starting point is the taboo of eating the liver. The toxicity of fugu liver has long been common knowledge, but on hearing that it is also incredibly delicious, many people have apparently given in to temptation and lost their lives. One of them was famed kabuki actor Bandō Mitsugorō VIII (1906–75). The living national treasure’s 1975 death by fugu poisoning resulted in a law strictly punishing the sale of fugu organs.
https://www.nippon.com/en/ncommon/contents/japan-topics/3079781/3079781.png
blocks.c: A traditional Ishikawa Prefecture dish of pickled fugu ovaries, which are just as dangerous as the liver. The only way to make them edible is this traditional method of fermenting them for over three years in brine and rice bran. (© Gun Fish Film Partners)

blocks.x: A traditional Ishikawa Prefecture dish of pickled fugu ovaries, which are just as dangerous as the liver. The only way to make them edible is this traditional method of fermenting them for over three years in brine and rice bran. (© Gun Fish Film Partners)
https://www.nippon.com/en/japan-topics/c030332/img/02_14989.jpg

But in 2004, a Nagasaki University research team investigating fugu poison succeeded in making farm-raised fugu poison-free, leading to an article in the English-language science magazine Nature. If fugu liver became safe to eat, it would surely mark a watershed moment in Japanese food culture.

Saga Prefecture sought to leverage this breakthrough in a local revitalization scheme. It applied to the MHLW for special certification as a Fugu Liver Zone, where people would be allowed to sell and eat nonpoisonous farmed fugu liver. Predictably, the National Fugu Federation and the city of Shimonoseki opposed the effort, saying a single accident could destroy trust in the nation’s fugu cuisine as a whole. The scheme has been rejected three times by the ministry and abandoned entirely.
The documentary takes up this liver-eating debate, introducing both the pro and anti sides as it explores the current state of fugu cuisine in Japan.

”I think if fugu weren’t poisonous, we wouldn’t have a movie. I see a certain Japanese-ness expressed in the opposing values that the debate brings to light. I wanted to show both sides equal respect, so I labeled them the ‘adventurers’ and the ‘custodians.’ Neither side is good nor bad; each is taking the stance of following through on their claims and their beliefs. And I find that really cool.”
https://www.nippon.com/en/ncommon/contents/japan-topics/3079782/3079782.jpg

blocks.x: Kamei Kazuhiro (right), owner chef of Kyoto restaurant Fugu Ryōri Tomoe, demonstrates the technique of slicing fugu sashimi. (© Gun Fish Film Partners)
Betting Their Lives on Fugu

The film introduces people working with fugu in all sorts of roles, each one sharing their own love of the fish. Their positions are all different, but they share the same ideals of broadening the dishes using this unique fish, preserving the culture of its cuisine, and nurturing it for the future.

Says the director: ”When I was editing the film, I grew convinced that bringing all of these people together into one film was something only I could do. That is one of the biggest things I learned through all this.”
https://www.nippon.com/en/ncommon/contents/japan-topics/3079783/3079783.png
blocks.c: Kitahama Kiichi, owner of Osaka’s Kitahachi restaurant and founder of the Fugu Museum, is one of the world’s leading fugu researchers. He insists that “Fugu brings people together.” (© Gun Fish Film Partners)

blocks.x: Kitahama Kiichi, owner of Osaka’s Kitahachi restaurant and founder of the Fugu Museum, is one of the world’s leading fugu researchers. He insists that “Fugu brings people together.” (© Gun Fish Film Partners)
In all, a decade passed from the start of filming until the documentary’s completion, spanning the COVID-19 pandemic.

Uno laughs: “Before I started looking into it, I had the same image of fugu as most, that it’s this poisonous, high-class fish. I never imagined I’d get so into it! This must be the true danger of fugu!”

items.text:
Veteran Indian actor Nana Patekar, known for his intense performances, has died at the age of 75 in Goa, his son Malhar told BBC Marathi.

One of the most recognisable faces of Indian cinema, Patekar won three National Film Awards and became known for playing complex, often volatile characters. He was also a prominent figure in Marathi language cinema and theatre.

He was admitted to a hospital after being found unconscious at his home in Goa in the early hours of Thursday.

"Despite 45 minutes of continuous CPR, he could not be revived," Dr Shekhar Salkar of Manipal Hospital in Goa told ANI news agency.

His funeral will take place later this evening with full state honours at his farm house in the western Indian city of Pune, the Maharashtra government has announced.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Narendra Modi led tributes to the actor, praising Patekar's versatility and outspoken personality.

Patekar portrayed characters that would "remain etched in the memory of generations", Modi wrote on X, adding that his death had left "a vast void in the artistic world".

Bollywood star Akshay Kumar, who appeared alongside Patekar in the comedy film Welcome, remembered him as a rare performer whose voice, intensity and honesty could command an audience's attention.

Patekar made his debut with the film Gaman in 1978 and continued to play smaller roles in several films. But the intensity that he brought on the screen was hard to miss and soon he landed a role in Parinda in 1989, making him a household name across India. He won his first National Film Award and the Filmfare Award as well for his portrayal of the gangster Anna in the film.

He didn't look back after this and portrayed many memorable roles in films in the 1990s. The range of characters he played showcased the depth of his acting talent and mastery of his craft.

Famous dialogues from his films, delivered in his inimitable raspy voice, were quoted in school corridors and tea stalls. Many professional comedians imitate his distinctive style even today.

"He had a distinctive style of working and how he approached characters. As a person, he was outspoken and difficult to get along with but directors would still want to work with him because he was simply a fantastic actor," film trade analyst Komal Nahta told BBC.

His portrayal of Major Chauhan in Prahaar – a film he also directed – won him praise. His other characters, including the patriotic hero of Tirangaa and Pratap Narayan Tilak in Krantiveer, also won him accolades.

Just when critics thought that playing loud characters was his mainstay, he proved them wrong by delivering a mesmerising performance in Khamoshi as a person who could not hear or speak.

Director Prakash Jha's Rajneeti in 2010 added another dimension to his acting as his portrayal of an astute politician was delivered with perfection.

The breadth of Patekar's career showcases the wide range of his work. He played different but contrasting roles like that of a notorious gangster or a policeman with equal ease. He also sometimes worked behind the camera as a director and writer.

His three national awards for Parinda, Krantiveer and Agni Sakshi are a also testament to his wide-ranging career.

Patekar was also an influential figure in both Marathi and Hindi theatre. Before making his debut in films, he was involved in theatre, where he developed his gritty style of dialogue delivery and also mastered the intensity he brought to his on-screen characters.

Purush and Hamidabai Chi Kothi were two of his most famous plays. Despite being successful in films, he remained active in theatre throughout his professional life.

Patekar was also known for his activism and didn't mince his words while criticising the government of the day. He was direct, and almost brazen and unapologetic, when it came to criticising ministers and their policies and that too quite publicly.

Issues related to farmers were particularly close to his heart.

His work also went beyond just giving statements. In 2015 he and actor Makarand Anaspure established the Naam Foundation, which has worked on farmer welfare and water conservation in Maharashtra.

But his career was not without controversies.

In 2018, allegations of sexual harassment made by actor Tanushree Dutta against Patekar over an alleged incident on a film set a decade earlier helped spark India's #MeToo movement. Patekar denied the allegations.

In 2019, he was cleared of the charges after police said they had not found sufficient evidence against him.

items.title: The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope
items.summary: As US President Donald Trump hits the campaign trail in the final sprint to the midterm elections, he is launching an emphatic defence of America's economic
items.text:
As US President Donald Trump hits the campaign trail in the final sprint to the midterm elections, he is launching an emphatic defence of America's economic performance, trying - as he often does - to bend reality to his will.

"We have the best economic numbers of any president in the history of our country, and yet people don't know about it because the press won't talk about it," he said last week.

While some economic indicators, including roaring stock market indexes and low US poverty rates, are indeed historic, the overall picture is not nearly as rosy.

Trump is often dismissive of concerns about aﬀordability and the high cost of living in the US, describing them as "fake" and a Democrat-inspired "hoax".

The American public, however, sees it differently - and some key economic indicators provide ample evidence for their discontent. Inflation remains high at 3.4%, outpacing wage growth. The average cost of petrol has soared to $4.37 (£3.30) a US gallon and beef prices are at a record high.

According to a YouGov survey, 63% of respondents believe the economy is "getting worse". An AP/NORC poll released last week found just 17% of adult Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall.

Those polls also suggest that many of Trump's policies, including tariffs, aggressive immigration enforcement and the ongoing conflict with Iran, are widely unpopular.

"We ask our voters their motivation to turn out, and what we find is cost of living, cost of living, cost of living," said Avery James, the director of communications at the Republican-aligned polling company Echelon Insights. "That's the top issue."

That has left Republicans running for office in the Congressional elections on 3 November with an agonising choice - should they be distancing themselves from Trump?

Their fear is that by echoing his sunny outlook they risk losing a number of electoral races that are currently projected to be very tight. But they also know that being seen to break with the president on the state of the economy is far from consequence free.

There are few Republican politicians as loyal to the president as Floridian House Congressman Byron Donalds. And there are few US states as traditionally hospitable to Republicans as Florida.

But even in the president's adopted home, which he carried in each of his three elections and which hasn't had a Democratic governor since 1999, candidates like Donalds are finding themselves having to adapt their pro-Republican messaging to acknowledge economic concerns.

Donalds - who stood by Trump as he fought his way back to power after his 2020 election defeat and took a prominent role in his 2024 election campaign - is now running for governor of Florida, with Trump's encouragement and enthusiastic endorsement.

When I saw him at a Hispanic church in Kissimmee, he was preaching to the proverbial choir - but pitching his message with a nod to the fact that for many money is currently tight.

"We're the best state in America," he said before acknowledging: "But success has gotten expensive."

He ticked through a laundry list of Florida constituents – retirees, teachers, emergency workers, restaurant staff and local government employees, flagging that they need to be able to "make ends meet".

In his stump speech, Donalds didn't mention Trump at all. He leaned heavily into stories of his own financial hardship during his younger years, of living paycheque to paycheque and waiting tables at the traditional southern style restaurant chain Cracker Barrel.

When he invited audience questions, there were the usual cultural hot-button topics, like the perceived threat of Sharia law in America, transgender athletes in women's sports and youth crime in public spaces.

But his supporters also wanted to talk about the high cost of housing - insurance, taxes, mortgage rates and home-owner fees - and healthcare worker shortages.

Trump may have mocked the term affordability, but Donalds – who is criss-crossing the state on an "affordability tour" – isn't the only Republican candidate talking about high prices.

It was a similar track at a campaign event in a Tampa seafood market the next day, when Bryan Avila, who is running for lieutenant governor on the same ticket as Donalds, took questions on energy prices and data centre construction.

"Everything is going up in prices, from food to even books for people going to college," said John Carroll, who serves on a Florida county housing commission. "It's a challenge no matter which party is in power, but here in Florida it's been Republican for so long."

Meanwhile in Texas, Governor Greg Abbott last month went to Texarkana to host a "rural affordability roundtable".

"We must lower costs for Texans in every corner of our state, and with my affordability agenda we will help make Texas the most affordable state in America."

And in Iowa, Ashley Hinson, a Republican congresswoman running for Senate, unveiled her own "affordability agenda".

"Iowans are paying the price for Washington's failures, and they deserve real relief that actually lowers costs," she said.

Hinson also recently called for the president to quickly end the Iran war – a sentiment echoed by Republican Senate candidates in Ohio and Michigan. Two of Hinson's Iowa colleagues in the House of Representatives went so far as to vote for a Democratic-backed measure to curtail Trump's war powers in Iran.

For the past two years it has been Republicans who control the levers of power in the nation's capital – from the White House to both chambers of Congress. Inevitably, that makes for a challenging rhetorical pirouette among Republican candidates this time round when it comes to touching on Trump's less popular policies.

Even Donalds has faced allegations that he is trying to open daylight between himself and Trump. The media was awash in reports recently that he had removed most prominent mentions of Trump from his campaign website.

It was a story Donalds quickly denied – and one that prompted an angry response from the president himself.

"Another Fake Story is that a very close friend of mine, a man I endorsed very early, Byron Donalds, is taking me off his website and campaign materials," Trump posted on his Truth Social website. "If Florida thought the story that Byron 'dropped' me was true, he would lose the election, and that would be a terrible thing because he's going to be a fantastic governor!"

Donalds did say, however, that when it comes to addressing how to tackle high prices, Trump shouldn't be a factor.

"That's not even about President Trump," he told reporters after the website story broke. "I'm the one asking for the votes for the people of Florida to be their governor."

While Donalds and Trump remain tight, the same cannot be said for Republican candidates who have gone farther in their criticism.

Congresswoman Maria Salazar aired a television spot in which she bluntly said Trump's immigration crackdown had "gone too far". Trump reposted a handful of messages on Truth Social accusing the Cuban-American Salazar of betrayal and calling for her to drop out, while other potential candidates had been on the receiving end of his anger during the primaries.

According to Marc Short, a Republican strategist and former chief of staff to Donald Trump's first vice-president, Mike Pence, it's hard not to see Trump's move as a warning directed at any other Republicans who might consider a public break with him. But he adds that Trump's ire isn't the only reason Republican candidates should approach this strategy with caution.

"It's almost disingenuous now to try to create separation," he says. "I think for voters it looks opportunistic."

Candidates like Salazar, who have stuck with Trump for years, have little choice but to rise and fall with the president's fortunes, he said. Republicans who have built their own brand and identities – like Senator Susan Collins in Maine – can more convincingly draw distinctions between themselves and the president.

The fact that so many people are downbeat about the economy, combined with the fact that the Republicans have been in power in Washington suggests that Republican candidates are facing difficult headwinds in November's elections. "I think they're hurricane force right now," said Short.

It is, however, far from a lost cause for Republicans going into these midterms. Many polls show battleground congressional and state races in a dead heat. And while Democratic candidates' hopes are buoyed by so many people feeling the economy is not working for them, a majority of voters still have a negative view of the Democratic Party as a whole.

"I think Republicans are closing out on the fact that they've delivered on a bunch of things, but we need to do more," said Alex DeGrasse, a Republican campaign consultant with close ties to the party's congressional leadership. His recommendation for the Republican electoral message was simple and pointed: "If you elect the Democrats, they'll destroy everything. Democrats had a chance to run the country, and by every objective economic metric, they did a worse job."

He added that right now in the White House, Republicans aren't panicking, they're focusing on executing their strategy.

In Florida's governor race, the Republican messaging contrasts the "Florida dream" of economic growth that Republicans say they delivered versus what they say is the hardship and depravity of Democratic-run states like Illinois, California and New York. Florida's population is booming, and many of the new arrivals are conservatives who lived in - and grew tired of - more liberal states in the north and west. But even this pitch often came with a nod to the current economic difficulties.

"For the past 26 years, we have been living in a Florida dream, and a lot of people don't realise the amount of work that has been done in this state," Avila said in Kissimmee last week.

According to James, from the Republican-aligned polling firm, the key for conservative candidates is to take subjects on which they are relatively strong, like crime, taxes and immigration, and link them to affordability issues that Americans say they care about most.

"Republicans are certainly looking to tell those independents that you might not be happy with everything, but we have delivered on these issues," he said.

With Republicans pouring money into advertising in battleground states, often outpacing their Democratic opponents by significant margins, there's still the possibility that the situation will improve in the final month of the midterm campaign.

That hasn't stopped the Republican faithful from being nervous about their side's chances, though – and what some see as a lack of enthusiasm on the right.

"Campaigns are won at the end by momentum," said Joseph Robinson, an engineer who attended the Avila fish-market event in Tampa. "But the momentum has been slow. It's not really like, 'Hey, I'm going to go run out there and vote right now.'"

Trump, for his part, is inevitably upbeat. Last month, he travelled to Tennessee for a college football game, where the crowd of more than 100,000 greeted him with cheers. The next day, it was a golf tournament in Illinois and another welcoming crowd. This weekend, he's going to another football game - in Alabama.

He is hitting the campaign trail, but frequently in states that mostly return Republican candidates – Texas, Oklahoma and Nebraska.

However, in classic Trump style, he is saying and doing things that could complicate the careful balancing act many Republicans are trying to strike.

He has repeatedly dismissed claims that high costs are a problem for many voters, with his latest explanation being that their discomfort is due to a "very bad job" on the part of his administration in explaining how good things really are.

"The only thing we're doing badly at is public relations," he said in Texas last week. "In other words, we're doing a phenomenal job."

Several times over the past few months he's insisted that voters imagine his name is "on the ballot", but at other times he has said he doesn't care about the midterms and that this isn't his election to fight.

If Republicans struggle, he said, it is not a reflection on how Americans view him.

"A lot of them are very angry at Republicans, to be honest with you," Trump said in August. "They're angry at Republicans, but they're not angry at me."

blocks.x: As US President Donald Trump hits the campaign trail in the final sprint to the midterm elections, he is launching an emphatic defence of America's economic performance, trying - as he often does - to bend reality to his will.
"We have the best economic numbers of any president in the history of our country, and yet people don't know about it because the press won't talk about it," he said last week.
While some economic indicators, including roaring stock market indexes and low US poverty rates, are indeed historic, the overall picture is not nearly as rosy.
Trump is often dismissive of concerns about aﬀordability and the high cost of living in the US, describing them as "fake" and a Democrat-inspired "hoax".

The American public, however, sees it differently - and some key economic indicators provide ample evidence for their discontent. Inflation remains high at 3.4%, outpacing wage growth. The average cost of petrol has soared to $4.37 (£3.30) a US gallon and beef prices are at a record high.

According to a YouGov survey, 63% of respondents believe the economy is "getting worse". An AP/NORC poll released last week found just 17% of adult Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall.
Those polls also suggest that many of Trump's policies, including tariffs, aggressive immigration enforcement and the ongoing conflict with Iran, are widely unpopular.

"We ask our voters their motivation to turn out, and what we find is cost of living, cost of living, cost of living," said Avery James, the director of communications at the Republican-aligned polling company Echelon Insights. "That's the top issue."
https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/8bc5/live/130a67b0-c166-11f1-babe-4199b0e7ccea.jpg
blocks.c: US President Trump holds a finger up at a rally

blocks.x: That has left Republicans running for office in the Congressional elections on 3 November with an agonising choice - should they be distancing themselves from Trump?

Their fear is that by echoing his sunny outlook they risk losing a number of electoral races that are currently projected to be very tight. But they also know that being seen to break with the president on the state of the economy is far from consequence free.
There are few Republican politicians as loyal to the president as Floridian House Congressman Byron Donalds. And there are few US states as traditionally hospitable to Republicans as Florida.

But even in the president's adopted home, which he carried in each of his three elections and which hasn't had a Democratic governor since 1999, candidates like Donalds are finding themselves having to adapt their pro-Republican messaging to acknowledge economic concerns.

Donalds - who stood by Trump as he fought his way back to power after his 2020 election defeat and took a prominent role in his 2024 election campaign - is now running for governor of Florida, with Trump's encouragement and enthusiastic endorsement.
When I saw him at a Hispanic church in Kissimmee, he was preaching to the proverbial choir - but pitching his message with a nod to the fact that for many money is currently tight.
"We're the best state in America," he said before acknowledging: "But success has gotten expensive."
https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/800/cpsprodpb/4f8c/live/4ecaf410-c164-11f1-bc2e-018d645d8d21.png
blocks.c: Anthony Zurcher

blocks.x: He ticked through a laundry list of Florida constituents – retirees, teachers, emergency workers, restaurant staff and local government employees, flagging that they need to be able to "make ends meet".

In his stump speech, Donalds didn't mention Trump at all. He leaned heavily into stories of his own financial hardship during his younger years, of living paycheque to paycheque and waiting tables at the traditional southern style restaurant chain Cracker Barrel.

When he invited audience questions, there were the usual cultural hot-button topics, like the perceived threat of Sharia law in America, transgender athletes in women's sports and youth crime in public spaces.
But his supporters also wanted to talk about the high cost of housing - insurance, taxes, mortgage rates and home-owner fees - and healthcare worker shortages.
Trump may have mocked the term affordability, but Donalds – who is criss-crossing the state on an "affordability tour" – isn't the only Republican candidate talking about high prices.

It was a similar track at a campaign event in a Tampa seafood market the next day, when Bryan Avila, who is running for lieutenant governor on the same ticket as Donalds, took questions on energy prices and data centre construction.

"Everything is going up in prices, from food to even books for people going to college," said John Carroll, who serves on a Florida county housing commission. "It's a challenge no matter which party is in power, but here in Florida it's been Republican for so long."
https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/cb55/live/9e1e2370-c191-11f1-a64c-550be9e3c66b.jpg
blocks.c: John Carroll

blocks.x: Meanwhile in Texas, Governor Greg Abbott last month went to Texarkana to host a "rural affordability roundtable".
"We must lower costs for Texans in every corner of our state, and with my affordability agenda we will help make Texas the most affordable state in America."
And in Iowa, Ashley Hinson, a Republican congresswoman running for Senate, unveiled her own "affordability agenda".
"Iowans are paying the price for Washington's failures, and they deserve real relief that actually lowers costs," she said.
https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/0d0e/live/d913acc0-c191-11f1-bc2e-018d645d8d21.jpg
blocks.c: Signs, one reads “Make Florida More Affordable."

blocks.x: Hinson also recently called for the president to quickly end the Iran war – a sentiment echoed by Republican Senate candidates in Ohio and Michigan. Two of Hinson's Iowa colleagues in the House of Representatives went so far as to vote for a Democratic-backed measure to curtail Trump's war powers in Iran.

For the past two years it has been Republicans who control the levers of power in the nation's capital – from the White House to both chambers of Congress. Inevitably, that makes for a challenging rhetorical pirouette among Republican candidates this time round when it comes to touching on Trump's less popular policies.

Even Donalds has faced allegations that he is trying to open daylight between himself and Trump. The media was awash in reports recently that he had removed most prominent mentions of Trump from his campaign website.
It was a story Donalds quickly denied – and one that prompted an angry response from the president himself.
https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/cb81/live/84ac5ef0-c166-11f1-a64c-550be9e3c66b.jpg
blocks.c: GOP candidate Byron Donalds speaks during a midterm campaign rally

blocks.x: "Another Fake Story is that a very close friend of mine, a man I endorsed very early, Byron Donalds, is taking me off his website and campaign materials," Trump posted on his Truth Social website. "If Florida thought the story that Byron 'dropped' me was true, he would lose the election, and that would be a terrible thing because he's going to be a fantastic governor!"
Donalds did say, however, that when it comes to addressing how to tackle high prices, Trump shouldn't be a factor.
"That's not even about President Trump," he told reporters after the website story broke. "I'm the one asking for the votes for the people of Florida to be their governor."
While Donalds and Trump remain tight, the same cannot be said for Republican candidates who have gone farther in their criticism.
https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/8af5/live/03a1be80-c167-11f1-bc2e-018d645d8d21.jpg
blocks.c: Officers patrol a US airport

blocks.x: Congresswoman Maria Salazar aired a television spot in which she bluntly said Trump's immigration crackdown had "gone too far". Trump reposted a handful of messages on Truth Social accusing the Cuban-American Salazar of betrayal and calling for her to drop out, while other potential candidates had been on the receiving end of his anger during the primaries.

According to Marc Short, a Republican strategist and former chief of staff to Donald Trump's first vice-president, Mike Pence, it's hard not to see Trump's move as a warning directed at any other Republicans who might consider a public break with him. But he adds that Trump's ire isn't the only reason Republican candidates should approach this strategy with caution.
"It's almost disingenuous now to try to create separation," he says. "I think for voters it looks opportunistic."

Candidates like Salazar, who have stuck with Trump for years, have little choice but to rise and fall with the president's fortunes, he said. Republicans who have built their own brand and identities – like Senator Susan Collins in Maine – can more convincingly draw distinctions between themselves and the president.

The fact that so many people are downbeat about the economy, combined with the fact that the Republicans have been in power in Washington suggests that Republican candidates are facing difficult headwinds in November's elections. "I think they're hurricane force right now," said Short.
https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/96ea/live/b786c0d0-c167-11f1-a64c-550be9e3c66b.jpg
blocks.c: President Trump surrounded by reporters as he departs the White House

blocks.x: It is, however, far from a lost cause for Republicans going into these midterms. Many polls show battleground congressional and state races in a dead heat. And while Democratic candidates' hopes are buoyed by so many people feeling the economy is not working for them, a majority of voters still have a negative view of the Democratic Party as a whole.

"I think Republicans are closing out on the fact that they've delivered on a bunch of things, but we need to do more," said Alex DeGrasse, a Republican campaign consultant with close ties to the party's congressional leadership. His recommendation for the Republican electoral message was simple and pointed: "If you elect the Democrats, they'll destroy everything. Democrats had a chance to run the country, and by every objective economic metric, they did a worse job."
He added that right now in the White House, Republicans aren't panicking, they're focusing on executing their strategy.

In Florida's governor race, the Republican messaging contrasts the "Florida dream" of economic growth that Republicans say they delivered versus what they say is the hardship and depravity of Democratic-run states like Illinois, California and New York. Florida's population is booming, and many of the new arrivals are conservatives who lived in - and grew tired of - more liberal states in the north and west. But even this pitch often came with a nod to the current economic difficulties.
"For the past 26 years, we have been living in a Florida dream, and a lot of people don't realise the amount of work that has been done in this state," Avila said in Kissimmee last week.

"Republicans are certainly looking to tell those independents that you might not be happy with everything, but we have delivered on these issues," he said.

Emma has dark-rimmed glasses, long fair hair and a striped shirt. John has short white hair with a white shirt and dark blazer. That hasn't stopped the Republican faithful from being nervous about their side's chances, though – and what some see as a lack of enthusiasm on the right.

"Campaigns are won at the end by momentum," said Joseph Robinson, an engineer who attended the Avila fish-market event in Tampa. "But the momentum has been slow. It's not really like, 'Hey, I'm going to go run out there and vote right now.'"

Trump, for his part, is inevitably upbeat. Last month, he travelled to Tennessee for a college football game, where the crowd of more than 100,000 greeted him with cheers. The next day, it was a golf tournament in Illinois and another welcoming crowd. This weekend, he's going to another football game - in Alabama.
He is hitting the campaign trail, but frequently in states that mostly return Republican candidates – Texas, Oklahoma and Nebraska.

He has repeatedly dismissed claims that high costs are a problem for many voters, with his latest explanation being that their discomfort is due to a "very bad job" on the part of his administration in explaining how good things really are.
"The only thing we're doing badly at is public relations," he said in Texas last week. "In other words, we're doing a phenomenal job."

Several times over the past few months he's insisted that voters imagine his name is "on the ballot", but at other times he has said he doesn't care about the midterms and that this isn't his election to fight.
If Republicans struggle, he said, it is not a reflection on how Americans view him.
"A lot of them are very angry at Republicans, to be honest with you," Trump said in August. "They're angry at Republicans, but they're not angry at me."

Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5: the cheapest, fastest, and most capable small model we’ve ever released.

Claude Haiku 5.5 is designed for high-volume, cost-sensitive tasks. It reliably handles quick and repetitive workloads (like summaries, compactions, database queries, and classification requests). It pairs well with Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 as a subagent on coding work. And, since it’s also our fastest model to date, it works especially well for speed-sensitive tasks like live customer support and browser use.¹

Haiku 5.5 is available at a much lower price than Haiku 4.5. On average, it now costs around 75% less to run.²

Along with this launch, we’re making improvements to the value of our model range. We’re halving the price of Claude Sonnet 5.5’s cache reads, which means Sonnet 5.5 now runs around 20% cheaper on most agentic work. And we’re introducing a new monthly API credit for our Claude Max and Team subscribers, designed to support our users in building new agents and applications that run on the Claude Platform.

Safety

Alignment. Claude Haiku 5.5 shows major improvements across almost all of our alignment evaluations relative to Haiku 4.5. In particular, we found far fewer instances of misaligned behavior, and a lower willingness to cooperate with misuse. The model’s system card describes our evaluation process and results in more detail.

Safeguards. Consistent with its capabilities, Haiku 5.5’s cybersecurity safeguards are more restrictive than Haiku 4.5’s, but somewhat less restrictive than those we’ve applied to other recent models. In cybersecurity, they permit a wider range of defensive tasks than our safeguards for Sonnet 5.5, but they still block penetration testing and other techniques more likely to be used by attackers.

Haiku 5.5’s biology safeguards are the same as for Sonnet 5, Sonnet 5.5, and Opus 5. They allow research biology questions but restrict access to requests that we judge as likely to cause harm. Organizations working on wider-ranging biology and cyber activities can apply to our Life Sciences Verification Program and Cyber Verification Program.

Availability

Claude Haiku 5.5 is available now on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. On the Claude Platform, developers can get started with claude-haiku-5-5.

See our migration guide for details.

Further updates

Alongside our new pricing for Claude Haiku 5.5, we’re making further improvements to the value of our models and products.

First, starting today, we’re lowering the price of cache reads on Claude Sonnet 5.5. Cache reads now cost 50% less: $0.10 per million tokens rather than $0.20. Because cache reads make up a large share of models’ token consumption, this reduces the cost of Sonnet 5.5 on most agentic tasks by around 20%.

Max 5x users will get $100 in credits per month, Max 20x users will get $200, and Team subscribers will receive up to $500, pooled across their users. These credits are designed to allow our users to experiment with building tools, apps, and agents that call our API. They can be used on any of our models. For developers, we’re also updating our Claude Python and TypeScript SDKs to add support for computer use and browser use in beta. Haiku 5.5 is especially well-suited to these tasks, given its combination of speed, capability, and price. You can read more about this in our Claude Platform docs.
